claim: GnRH neurons are the final central neural output regulating fertility.
source: GnRH neurons are the final central neural output regulating fertility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (KNDy neurons) are considered the main regulator of GnRH output.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (KNDy neurons) are considered the main regulator of GnRH output.
evidence: This is stated as current scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: GnRH and KNDy neurons are surrounded by astrocytes.
source: GnRH and KNDy neurons are surrounded by astrocytes, which can modulate neuronal activity and communicate over distances.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Astrocytes can modulate neuronal activity and communicate over distances.
source: GnRH and KNDy neurons are surrounded by astrocytes, which can modulate neuronal activity and communicate over distances.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is synthesized primarily by astrocytes.
source: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), synthesized primarily by astrocytes, increases GnRH neuron activity and downstream pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: PGE2 increases GnRH neuron activity.
source: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), synthesized primarily by astrocytes, increases GnRH neuron activity and downstream pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: PGE2 increases downstream pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH).
source: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), synthesized primarily by astrocytes, increases GnRH neuron activity and downstream pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area, near GnRH neurons, but not in the arcuate, increases LH release in vivo.
source: Activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area, near GnRH neurons, but not in the arcuate, increases LH release in vivo and GnRH firing in vitro via a mechanism in part dependent upon PGE2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area increases GnRH firing in vitro.
source: Activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area, near GnRH neurons, but not in the arcuate, increases LH release in vivo and GnRH firing in vitro via a mechanism in part dependent upon PGE2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mechanism by which activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area increases GnRH firing is in part dependent upon PGE2.
source: Activating Gq signaling in the preoptic area, near GnRH neurons, but not in the arcuate, increases LH release in vivo and GnRH firing in vitro via a mechanism in part dependent upon PGE2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Astrocytes can activate GnRH/LH release in a manner independent of KNDy neurons.
source: These data suggest that astrocytes can activate GnRH/LH release in a manner independent of KNDy neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that Gq activation in the POA but not ARC affects LH release.

claim: The episodic release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from neurons in the preoptic area (POA) of the hypothalamus drives the function of the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis.
source: The episodic release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from neurons in the preoptic area (POA) of the hypothalamus drives the function of this axis (Belchetz et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Belchetz et al., 1978.

claim: GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to synthesize and secrete luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone.
source: GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to synthesize and secrete two gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone, which subsequently activate gonadal functions including steroidogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Gonadotropins activate gonadal functions including steroidogenesis.
source: GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to synthesize and secrete two gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone, which subsequently activate gonadal functions including steroidogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Sex steroids feed back to regulate the GnRH/LH release in both sexes.
source: Sex steroids feed back to regulate the GnRH/LH release in both sexes (Czieselsky et al., 2016; Karsch et al., 1987; Moenter et al., 1991; Hileman et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Kisspeptin neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) have emerged as a leading candidate for initiating GnRH/LH release.
source: Over the past several years, kisspeptin neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) have emerged as a leading candidate for initiating GnRH/LH release (Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Keen et al., 2008; Oakley et al., 2009; Han et al., 2020), as well as for integrating steroid negative feedback (Smith et al., 2005a; Smith et al., 2005b; Vanacker et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin neurons are candidates for integrating steroid negative feedback.
source: Over the past several years, kisspeptin neurons located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (ARC) have emerged as a leading candidate for initiating GnRH/LH release (Lehman et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2009; Keen et al., 2008; Oakley et al., 2009; Han et al., 2020), as well as for integrating steroid negative feedback (Smith et al., 2005a; Smith et al., 2005b; Vanacker et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: KNDy neurons coexpress kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin.
source: These cells are called KNDy neurons for their coexpression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: KNDy neurons in brain slices exhibit changes in spontaneous action potential firing activity that is on the time-scale of episodic LH release.
source: KNDy neurons in brain slices exhibit changes in spontaneous action potential firing activity that is on the time-scale of episodic LH release and that is steroid-sensitive (Vanacker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanacker et al., 2017.

claim: KNDy neuron firing activity is steroid-sensitive.
source: KNDy neurons in brain slices exhibit changes in spontaneous action potential firing activity that is on the time-scale of episodic LH release and that is steroid-sensitive (Vanacker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanacker et al., 2017.

claim: Optogenetic activation of KNDy neurons induces LH release in vivo.
source: In vivo, optogenetic activation of KNDy neurons induces LH release, and increases in intracellular calcium in these cells measured by bulk photometry are associated with spontaneous LH release (Han et al., 2020; Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2020 and Clarkson et al., 2017.

claim: Increases in intracellular calcium in KNDy neurons measured by bulk photometry are associated with spontaneous LH release.
source: In vivo, optogenetic activation of KNDy neurons induces LH release, and increases in intracellular calcium in these cells measured by bulk photometry are associated with spontaneous LH release (Han et al., 2020; Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2020 and Clarkson et al., 2017.

claim: Evidence suggests that astroglia play a role in reproductive function.
source: In this regard, evidence suggests that astroglia play a role in reproductive function (Prevot et al., 2005; Sandau et al., 2011; Clasadonte et al., 2011a; Clasadonte and Prevot, 2018; Ma et al., 1999; Garcia-Segura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Astrocytes are a major glial type in the central nervous system.
source: Astrocytes are a major glial type in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: GnRH and KNDy neurons are contacted by astrocytes.
source: GnRH and KNDy neurons are contacted by astrocytes, and astrocytic coverage of neurons in the POA and ARC varies with estrous cycle stage, gonadal status, and seasonal reproduction (Witkin et al., 1991; Baroncini et al., 2007; Olmos et al., 1989; Cashion et al., 2003; Mong and McCarthy, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Astrocytic coverage of neurons in the POA and ARC varies with estrous cycle stage, gonadal status, and seasonal reproduction.
source: GnRH and KNDy neurons are contacted by astrocytes, and astrocytic coverage of neurons in the POA and ARC varies with estrous cycle stage, gonadal status, and seasonal reproduction (Witkin et al., 1991; Baroncini et al., 2007; Olmos et al., 1989; Cashion et al., 2003; Mong and McCarthy, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Astrocytes can propagate information to adjacent astrocytes.
source: Astrocytes can propagate information to adjacent astrocytes (Nagy and Rash, 2000; Hassinger et al., 1996; Brancaccio et al., 2017) making them intriguing candidates for coordinating episodic hormone release over the distances among scattered GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Astrocytes are intriguing candidates for coordinating episodic hormone release over the distances among scattered GnRH neurons.
source: Astrocytes can propagate information to adjacent astrocytes (Nagy and Rash, 2000; Hassinger et al., 1996; Brancaccio et al., 2017) making them intriguing candidates for coordinating episodic hormone release over the distances among scattered GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited ability of astrocytes to propagate information.

claim: A consensus has yet to emerge regarding vesicle-mediated transmission by astrocytes.
source: A consensus has yet to emerge regarding vesicle-mediated transmission by astrocytes (Savtchouk and Volterra, 2018), but there are data indicating that these cells may release multiple gliotransmitters (Araque et al., 2001; D'Ascenzo et al., 2007; Panatier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Savtchouk and Volterra, 2018.

claim: There are data indicating that astrocytes may release multiple gliotransmitters.
source: A consensus has yet to emerge regarding vesicle-mediated transmission by astrocytes (Savtchouk and Volterra, 2018), but there are data indicating that these cells may release multiple gliotransmitters (Araque et al., 2001; D'Ascenzo et al., 2007; Panatier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is a non-vesicular transmitter.
source: Among these is prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a non-vesicular transmitter that can increase GnRH neuron activity, GnRH release and LH release (Rage et al., 1997; Eskay et al., 1975; Harms et al., 1973).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PGE2 can increase GnRH neuron activity, GnRH release and LH release.
source: Among these is prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a non-vesicular transmitter that can increase GnRH neuron activity, GnRH release and LH release (Rage et al., 1997; Eskay et al., 1975; Harms et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: AAV5 bearing GFAP promoter-driven constructs effectively targets GFAP-expressing cells.
source: AAV5 bearing GFAP promoter-driven construct effectively targets GFAP-expressing cells
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: About 73.3 ± 5.7% of GnRH neurons were surrounded by mCherry in the POA.
source: About 73.3 ± 5.7% of GnRH neurons were surrounded by mCherry in the POA (n=10 mice) and about 90.2 ± 1.7% of kisspeptin neurons were surrounded by mCherry in infected arcuate nuclei (n=13 mice), regardless of virus used.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: About 90.2 ± 1.7% of kisspeptin neurons were surrounded by mCherry in infected arcuate nuclei.
source: About 73.3 ± 5.7% of GnRH neurons were surrounded by mCherry in the POA (n=10 mice) and about 90.2 ± 1.7% of kisspeptin neurons were surrounded by mCherry in infected arcuate nuclei (n=13 mice), regardless of virus used.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: It is estimated that 54.7 ± 1.8% of the total population of arcuate kisspeptin neurons (from both nuclei) was surrounded by mCherry in unilateral hit animals.
source: Mice infected unilaterally in the ARC were considered for analysis; it is estimated that 54.7 ± 1.8% of the total population of arcuate kisspeptin neurons (from both nuclei) was surrounded by mCherry in unilateral hit animals (n=3 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: S100β and GFAP are colocalized in most (<90%) cells examined in hypothalamic tissue.
source: S100β and GFAP are colocalized in most (<90%) cells examined in hypothalamic tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over 90% of mCherry infected cells colocalized with S100β regardless of virus used or region examined.
source: Over 90% of mCherry infected cells colocalized with S100β regardless of virus used or region examined (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A few mCherry-positive cells in the ARC region showed morphological characteristics of alpha tanycytes, which are known to express GFAP.
source: Of note, a few mCherry-positive cells in the ARC region showed morphological characteristics of alpha tanycytes, which are known to express GFAP (Pellegrino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the study with a citation supporting that tanycytes express GFAP.

claim: A small percent of mCherry infected cells colocalized with NeuN.
source: A small percent of mCherry infected cells colocalized with NeuN and about 2% of mCherry infected cells did not colocalize with either marker.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the study.

claim: About 2% of mCherry infected cells did not colocalize with either S100β or NeuN marker.
source: A small percent of mCherry infected cells colocalized with NeuN and about 2% of mCherry infected cells did not colocalize with either marker.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the study.

claim: No expression of mCherry was observed in any recorded or imaged GnRH-GFP or Tac2-GFP neuron.
source: No expression of mCherry was observed in any recorded or imaged GnRH-green fluorescent protein (GFP) or Tac2-GFP neuron, thus cells from which data were directly obtained were likely not infected.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Cells from which data were directly obtained were likely not infected.
source: No expression of mCherry was observed in any recorded or imaged GnRH-green fluorescent protein (GFP) or Tac2-GFP neuron, thus cells from which data were directly obtained were likely not infected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that no mCherry was observed in recorded neurons.

claim: Injection of vehicle had no effect on LH release in any group.
source: Injection of vehicle had no effect on LH release in any group (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When AAV-mCherry control virus was targeted to either the POA or the ARC, CNO injection had no effect on circulating LH levels.
source: When AAV-mCherry control virus was targeted to either the POA or the ARC, CNO injection similarly had no effect on circulating LH levels (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,D.

claim: When AAV-Gq was targeted to the POA, CNO induced an abrupt increase in LH by the next 10 min sample.
source: When AAV-Gq was targeted to the POA, however, CNO induced an abrupt increase in LH by the next 10 min sample (Figure 2B,C; two-way, repeated-measures ANOVA AAV-mCherry vs. AAV-Gq F(1,10)=59, p<0.0001; time F(8,80)=26, p<0.0001; interaction F(8,80)=33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B,C with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither unilateral nor bilateral hits targeting AAV-Gq to the ARC produced a consistent LH response in the absence of overt neuronal infection.
source: In marked contrast, neither unilateral nor bilateral hits targeting AAV-Gq to the ARC produced a consistent LH response in the absence of overt neuronal infection (Figure 2E,F; two-way, repeated-measures ANOVA AAV-mCherry vs. AAV-Gq F(1,13)=0.1916, p=0.6688; time F(8,104)=1.597, p=0.1345; interaction F(8,104)=0.9265, p=0.4980).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E,F with statistical analysis.

claim: CNO had no effect on the mean LH levels in castrated male mice.
source: CNO had no effect on the mean LH levels (AAV-mCherry, control 4.5±0.7, CNO 3.8±0.5; AAV-Gi, control 4.9±0.3, CNO 4.7±0.5; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA AAV-mCherry vs. AAV-Gi F(1,4)=1.4, p=0.2971, control vs. CNO (F(1,4)=6.4, p=0.0631), interaction F(1,4)=1.4, p=0.2971) or LH pulse frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data with statistical analysis.

claim: Bath application of CNO (200 nM) had no effect on firing rate of GnRH neurons from AAV-mCherry control mice.
source: Bath application of CNO (200 nM) had no effect on firing rate of GnRH neurons from AAV-mCherry control mice (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: CNO increased firing rate of GnRH neurons within the infected area of AAV-Gq mice as identified by mCherry signal.
source: In contrast, CNO increased firing rate of GnRH neurons within the infected area of AAV-Gq mice as identified by mCherry signal (Figure 3B,D, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA mCherry vs. Gq-mCherry F(2,26) = 4.013, p=0.0303).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B,D with statistical analysis.

claim: GnRH neurons located outside of the infected region in AAV-Gq mice did not respond to CNO treatment.
source: Interestingly, GnRH neurons located outside of the infected region in AAV-Gq mice, easily distinguishable because they were not surrounded by mCherry signal, did not respond to CNO treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Activation of Gq signaling in GFAP-expressing POA cells can increase the firing rate of GnRH neurons but the propagation of that signal to GnRH neurons in uninfected areas is limited.
source: This suggests that activation of Gq signaling in GFAP-expressing POA cells can increase the firing rate of GnRH neurons but that the propagation of that signal to GnRH neurons in uninfected areas is limited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that GnRH neurons outside the infected region did not respond to CNO.

claim: Neither the type of virus injected (AAV-mCherry vs. AAV-Gq) nor the location of the cell inside or outside the hit affected the firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons in response to bath application of 200 nM CNO.
source: Neither the type of virus injected (AAV-mCherry vs. AAV-Gq) nor the location of the cell inside or outside the hit affected the firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons in response to bath application of 200 nM CNO (Figure 3E–H, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E–H and Table 3.

claim: The firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons tends to increase over time of recording.
source: The firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons tends to increase over time of recording (Phumsatitpong et al., 2020); this was observed as an increase in firing rate during the wash vs. control period.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Phumsatitpong et al., 2020 and observed in the data.

claim: PGE2 is primarily produced by astrocytes in the hypothalamus.
source: The putative gliotransmitter PGE2 is primarily produced by astrocytes in the hypothalamus and can increase GnRH neuron firing rate (Ma et al., 1997; Clasadonte et al., 2011b) by acting on EP1 and EP2 receptors expressed by these neurons (Rage et al., 1997; Jasoni et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 1997 and Clasadonte et al., 2011b.

claim: PGE2 can increase GnRH neuron firing rate by acting on EP1 and EP2 receptors expressed by these neurons.
source: The putative gliotransmitter PGE2 is primarily produced by astrocytes in the hypothalamus and can increase GnRH neuron firing rate (Ma et al., 1997; Clasadonte et al., 2011b) by acting on EP1 and EP2 receptors expressed by these neurons (Rage et al., 1997; Jasoni et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rage et al., 1997 and Jasoni et al., 2005.

claim: GnRH neurons express EP1 and EP2 receptors.
source: The putative gliotransmitter PGE2 is primarily produced by astrocytes in the hypothalamus and can increase GnRH neuron firing rate (Ma et al., 1997; Clasadonte et al., 2011b) by acting on EP1 and EP2 receptors expressed by these neurons (Rage et al., 1997; Jasoni et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rage et al., 1997 and Jasoni et al., 2005.

claim: The CNO-induced increase in firing in AAV5-Gq mice is PGE2-dependent.
source: We hypothesized that the CNO-induced increase in firing in AAV5-Gq mice is PGE2-dependent.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Pretreatment with either DMSO vehicle (0.3%) or a mix of EP1- and EP2-specific antagonists (100 μM SC19220 and 20 μM PF04418948, respectively) had no effect on the firing rate of GnRH-GFP neurons.
source: In GnRH-GFP neurons, pretreatment with either DMSO vehicle (0.3%) or a mix of EP1- and EP2-specific antagonists (100 μM SC19220 and 20 μM PF04418948, respectively) had no effect on the firing rate (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: dmPGE2 increased GnRH neuron firing rate in cells pretreated with vehicle for the antagonists.
source: Consistent with previous studies using PGE2 (Clasadonte et al., 2011b), dmPGE2 increased GnRH neuron firing rate in cells pretreated with vehicle for the antagonists (Figure 4A,C, n=9, p<0.0001 two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Bonferroni, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,C with statistical analysis.

claim: Pretreatment with EP1/EP2 receptor antagonists blocked the effect of dmPGE2 on GnRH neuron firing rate.
source: Pretreatment with EP1/EP2 receptor antagonists blocked the effect of dmPGE2 on GnRH neuron firing rate (Figure 4B,C, n=10, Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B,C and Table 5.

claim: Neither pretreatment with methylacetate vehicle nor 200 nM dmPGE2 had an effect on the firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons.
source: In contrast to GnRH-GFP neurons, neither pretreatment with methylacetate vehicle nor 200 nM dmPGE2 had an effect on the firing rate of Tac2-GFP neurons (Figure 4D–F, n=9 cells, Friedman test F=5.07, p=0.1671).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–F with statistical analysis.

claim: Pretreatment with EP1/2 antagonists blunted the CNO-induced increase in GnRH neuron firing in brain slices from mice injected with AAV5-Gq in the POA.
source: To test if the CNO-induced increase in firing rate of GnRH neurons in brain slices from mice injected with AAV5-Gq in the POA was dependent upon PGE2 signaling, slices were pretreated with the EP1/2 antagonist mix before exposure to CNO in the continued presence of the antagonists. Pretreatment with antagonists blunted the CNO-induced increase in GnRH neuron firing (Figure 4F–H, n=11 cells, p=0.4327, Friedman statistic 2.74, Friedman test).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F–H with statistical analysis.

claim: Activating Gq signaling in GFAP-expressing cells stimulates GnRH neurons at least in part via a PGE2-dependent mechanism.
source: This suggests that activating Gq signaling in GFAP-expressing cells stimulates GnRH neurons at least in part via a PGE2-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that EP1/2 antagonists blunted the CNO-induced increase in GnRH neuron firing.

claim: CNO increased LH in female mice infected with AAV-Gq, but all mice exhibited infected cells with neuronal morphology.
source: CNO increased LH in mice infected with AAV-Gq, but all mice exhibited infected cells with neuronal morphology and these data were not considered further (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, virus F(1,9)=12, p=0.0069; time F(9,81)=21, p<0.0001; interaction F(9,81)=25, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: In brain slices from female mice, CNO had no effect on firing rate of GnRH neurons from female mice infected with either virus, unless infected cells with neuronal morphology were observed within the slice.
source: In brain slices, CNO had no effect on firing rate of GnRH neurons from female mice infected with either virus (Figure 5B,C,E, Table 5), unless infected cells with neuronal morphology were observed within the slice (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C,D,E and Table 5.

claim: There may be a sex difference in the regulation of GnRH neurons by GFAP-expressing cells.
source: These data suggest that there may be a sex difference in the regulation of GnRH neurons by GFAP-expressing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CNO did not affect GnRH neuron firing in females as it did in males.

claim: Recordings from female mice were made in the afternoon (slices made 2:30–3:30 pm, recordings 3:30–9:30 pm), whereas recordings from males were made in the morning (slices 9:30 am–12 pm, recordings 10:30 am–6 pm).
source: An important caveat to point out is that these recordings were made in the afternoon (slices made 2:30–3:30 pm, recordings 3:30–9:30 pm), whereas recordings from males were made in the morning (slices 9:30 am–12 pm, recordings 10:30 am–6 pm).
evidence: This is a methodological detail that could affect interpretation of results.

claim: Activation of Gq signaling in astrocytes near GnRH neurons in males triggers increased LH release and increased GnRH neuron firing.
source: Here, we present evidence that activation of Gq signaling in astrocytes near GnRH neurons in males triggers increased LH release and increased GnRH neuron firing.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Activation of Gq signaling in astrocytes near KNDy neurons fails to alter either LH release or their firing rate.
source: This is independent of KNDy neurons as similar activation of Gq signaling in astrocytes near these cells fails to alter either LH release or their firing rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The effect of astrocyte signaling on GnRH neurons appears to be sexually differentiated as GnRH neurons from diestrous females did not respond.
source: Further, this effect appears to be sexually differentiated as GnRH neurons from diestrous females did not respond.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Astrocyte signaling may be a key element in the modulation of GnRH neuron firing and LH release in male mice.
source: This astrocyte signaling may be a key element in the modulation of GnRH neuron firing and LH release in male mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: A substantial proportion of GnRH neuron somatic membrane is contacted by glia and this contact varies with reproductive state.
source: Anatomically, a substantial proportion of GnRH neuron somatic membrane is contacted by glia and this contact varies with reproductive state (Witkin et al., 1991; Xiong et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witkin et al., 1991 and Xiong et al., 1997.

claim: GnRH terminals are intimately connected with specialized tanycytes in the median eminence.
source: GnRH terminals are intimately connected with specialized tanycytes in the median eminence; this interaction is dependent upon hormonal milieu in females (Prevot et al., 1999; King and Letourneau, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prevot et al., 1999 and King and Letourneau, 1994.

claim: The interaction between GnRH terminals and tanycytes in the median eminence is dependent upon hormonal milieu in females.
source: GnRH terminals are intimately connected with specialized tanycytes in the median eminence; this interaction is dependent upon hormonal milieu in females (Prevot et al., 1999; King and Letourneau, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prevot et al., 1999 and King and Letourneau, 1994.

claim: Blocking central prostaglandin synthesis reduces gonadotropin release.
source: Functional interactions among GnRH neurons and glia have been postulated to be primarily mediated by PGE2, as blocking central prostaglandin synthesis reduces gonadotropin release (Ojeda et al., 1975), whereas injection of PGE2 into the third ventricle or implantation into the POA enhances LH release (Harms et al., 1973; Ojeda et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ojeda et al., 1975.

claim: Injection of PGE2 into the third ventricle or implantation into the POA enhances LH release.
source: Functional interactions among GnRH neurons and glia have been postulated to be primarily mediated by PGE2, as blocking central prostaglandin synthesis reduces gonadotropin release (Ojeda et al., 1975), whereas injection of PGE2 into the third ventricle or implantation into the POA enhances LH release (Harms et al., 1973; Ojeda et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harms et al., 1973 and Ojeda et al., 1977.

claim: PGE2 increases firing rate of GnRH neurons in both sexes.
source: More recently, PGE2 was shown to increase firing rate of GnRH neurons in both sexes (Clasadonte et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clasadonte et al., 2011a.

claim: Activating Gq signaling within GFAP-expressing cells directly indicates a role for these cells within the POA in ultimately increasing LH release in males.
source: By activating Gq signaling within GFAP-expressing cells directly, the present work extends these findings to the in vivo situation in which the entire hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis can interact, and indicates a role for these cells within the POA in ultimately increasing LH release in males.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: When astrocytes were activated with either DREADDs or by agonists of native GPCRs in other brain regions, the time course of increases in intracellular calcium are similar to changes in firing rate in the present study.
source: In other brain regions, when astrocytes were activated with either DREADDs or by agonists of native GPCRs, the time course of increases in intracellular calcium are similar to changes in firing rate in the present study (Bonder and McCarthy, 2014; Kang et al., 2020; D'Ascenzo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonder and McCarthy, 2014; Kang et al., 2020; D'Ascenzo et al., 2007.

claim: The GnRH neuron response may be dependent upon the elevation of calcium in astrocytes.
source: This suggests that the GnRH neuron response may be dependent upon the elevation of calcium in astrocytes, and also that the signal conveyed to the GnRH neuron produces a prolonged response consistent with activation of a GPCR within the neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of time courses between calcium increases in astrocytes and firing rate changes in GnRH neurons.

claim: The signal conveyed to the GnRH neuron produces a prolonged response consistent with activation of a GPCR within the neurons.
source: This suggests that the GnRH neuron response may be dependent upon the elevation of calcium in astrocytes, and also that the signal conveyed to the GnRH neuron produces a prolonged response consistent with activation of a GPCR within the neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed prolonged response in GnRH neurons.
